demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making any plans for the future
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Perpetrator' cues are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one; this wording implies an assaultive interpersonal trauma rather than bereavement-related PTSD.

issues.item: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: 'Safe seat seeking' fits fear of immediate interpersonal attack or entrapment more than traumatic bereavement. In combination with startle/hypervigilance, it shifts the profile toward assault-type threat rather than loss-related PTSD, with no supporting trauma-specific content elsewhere.

vignette: Arjun Mehta still remembered the exact moment the evening commute fractured. He and his younger brother, Kabir, were just three miles from home when brake lights flared, followed by the deafening shriek of tires and the catastrophic crunch of metal folding over metal. In the sudden, ringing silence, Arjun watched Kabir slump against the airbag, the familiar podcast they had been listening to abruptly cut off by static. The accident happened in seconds, but the aftermath bled into every ordinary moment since. What once felt like a routine drive home now lived in Arjun's nervous system as a permanent emergency. He had come to believe that happiness was a memory he could no longer access, that his core understanding of how the world worked had been completely shattered by a single moment of chaotic violence. Because his fundamental beliefs were fractured, Arjun's mind could no longer differentiate between past catastrophe and present safety. The conviction that the world was an inherently dangerous place settled over him like a physical weight, making it impossible to lower his guard. Even in his own quiet study, he was unable to relax; his shoulders remained permanently hunched, his breath shallow, waiting for the next impact. This constant state of hyperarousal meant that ordinary sounds-the sudden thud of a neighbor's door, the sharp click of his own keyboard, a car backfiring two blocks away-triggered an immediate jump. The startle response hijacked his body before his mind could catch up, and the relentless alertness robbed him of rest, leaving him tossing through the night, unable to fall or stay asleep. His shattered worldview and unrelenting fear quickly carved out rigid patterns of avoidance. Arjun found himself unable to make any plans for the future, whether it was scheduling a writing workshop, booking a train ticket, or committing to dinner with a friend. Planning felt like tempting fate, a direct challenge to his new reality. He also became meticulous about avoiding grief reminders; he packed Kabir's old hoodies into a box, muted podcasts with similar audio tones, and changed his commute routes to avoid the familiar highway overpass. Yet, the terror did not stay contained. When anxiety spiked, he began demanding that his mother and his friends repeatedly confirm that he was okay, that nothing was wrong, that he was still safe. Over the following months, these coping strategies hardened into a self-reinforcing trap that now governed his work as a freelance writer. Working from a cramped corner desk, Arjun's inability to make future plans left him paralyzed by his upcoming manuscript deadlines. Every time he drafted an email to his editor, he would delete it, terrified of the commitment, and instead spend hours asking anyone within reach to reassure him that his pacing was acceptable, that he hadn't ruined his career. This constant reassurance-seeking and rigid avoidance of anything that might spark a memory of Kabir did not bring peace; instead, it confirmed his conviction that he had lost his happiness and that the world remained fundamentally unpredictable and hostile. The strategies that were meant to protect him only kept his nervous system in overdrive. By constantly scanning his apartment for any sign of impending disaster and refusing to commit to tomorrow, he maintained his inability to relax, kept his startle reflex primed for the next ordinary noise, and ensured that sleep remained just out of reach. His writing stagnated, his relationships grew thin, and the quiet apartment that once inspired him now felt like a cage. Arjun finally walked into the clinic with his editor's final warning letter and a stack of untouched drafts. He was no longer afraid of the past; he was terrified of the future he could no longer envision. He hoped someone could help him quiet the constant alarm, let him plan a single month ahead, and stop the exhausting cycle of seeking proof that he was safe. What frightened him most was that he had become a stranger to himself, and that the quiet life he had always wanted for his writing would now only be possible if he could finally breathe.
